The fear was not a settled scientific “conclusion.” During the Manhattan Project, physicists had never detonated a nuclear weapon and had only partial, uncertain models of what a nuclear fireball would do. Some worried that if the explosion’s fireball heated the surrounding air strongly enough, it might “set the atmosphere on fire” or trigger some kind of runaway atmospheric ignition. The idea that the atmosphere would “burn up in mere moments” mostly comes from early worst-case, back-of-the-envelope reasoning — often associated with Robert Oppenheimer’s unease — not from a rigorous, validated calculation showing the whole sky would ignite.

In physical terms, the fear was an overcautious extrapolation. A 1945 atomic bomb released about 20 kilotons of energy, which is enormous for a weapon, but still tiny compared with the total heat capacity of Earth’s atmosphere. Air is also not a fuel in the way wood or gasoline is; it contains oxygen, not a fuel source, and a nuclear fireball rapidly expands, radiates away energy, and cools rather than propagating as a global chemical fire. After the Trinity test and more careful calculations, it was clear that a nuclear detonation would not burn up the atmosphere in moments. So the “conclusion” was really an early miscalculation or dramatic fear born of incomplete knowledge, not a proven prediction.
